label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 3 — Psalms 42–72
summary_plain: Psalms 42 through 72 contain the prayers of the Korachites and Dawid in exile and hope. Psalm 42 opens: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O YHWH. Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song. Psalm 46 declares: YHWH of hosts is with us — the Creator of Ya'aqov is our refuge. Psalm 51 is Dawid's plea for a clean heart after his sin: Create in me a clean heart, O Creator, and renew a right spirit within me. Psalm 68 exalts YHWH as the Rider on the Clouds — his name is YAH. Psalm 72 closes with a prayer for the righteous king and the declaration: Blessed be YHWH, the Creator of Yisra'EL, who alone does wondrous things.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalms 42-72 from DSS witnesses and the Orit Ge'ez. Psalm 51 is critical for understanding teshuvah (return/repentance) in the covenant framework — Dawid does not seek a priestly sacrifice but a direct encounter with YHWH: 'The sacrifices of The Creator are a broken spirit — a broken and contrite heart, O Creator, you will not despise' (51:17). This is the covenant relationship without institutional mediation. Psalm 68:4 applies the title Rider on the Clouds (Rokev ba-Aravot) to YHWH and names him YAH. This same title — Rkb 'rpt — appears in the Ugaritic Baal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1-1.6, c. 1300 BCE) as the primary epithet of Baal. The Hebrew tradition reclaimed this Afro-Asiatic title and applied it to YHWH — the true Rider on the Clouds. The Elohistic Psalter (42-83) uses Elohim more frequently than YHWH, suggesting an editorial layer that substituted the title for the personal name.

key_terms.definition: Asaph's near-collapse of faith when he saw the prosperity of the wicked — 'their bodies are fat and sleek, they are not in trouble as others are.' The resolution comes in the sanctuary when he sees their destiny. Begins Book III of Tehillim.

Asaph's long teaching psalm recounting Yisra'el's history of rebellion and YHWH's patient faithfulness from Mitzrayim through the wilderness to the choice of David. The longest historical psalm in Tehillim.

'YHWH stands in the divine assembly; in the midst of the elohim he judges.' This ancient Hebrew text documents the concept of a divine council from primary Hebrew sources — YHWH presiding as judge over assembled divine beings.

YHWH addresses the council members (elohim) who have failed to execute justice for the poor and weak. YHWH pronounces their mortality as judgment. NT writers borrowed Ps.82:6 ('you are elohim, sons of the Most High') for a different theological claim; the original context is a court judgment condemning failed divine-council members.

'I said, you are elohim, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince.' YHWH addressing the council members whose privilege is revoked. Ancient source; NT borrowed this verse.

Ethan the Ezrahite's psalm affirming the Davidic covenant — YHWH's sworn oath to maintain David's line forever. The psalm moves from exaltation to deep lament when YHWH appears to have abandoned the covenant.

Author of Psalm 89 according to its superscription; listed in 1 Kings 5:11 as a wise man surpassed only by Shlomo. His psalm stands at the end of Book III, closing it with a lament about the apparent failure of the Davidic covenant promise.

Levitical musician appointed by David (1 Chronicles 15:17); 12 psalms in Tehillim are attributed to Asaph (Ps.50, 73-83). His psalms often engage historical reflection, divine council imagery, and wrestling with the problem of evil.

A Levitical guild descended from Korakh (Bamidbar 16); 11 psalms attributed to them (Ps.42-49, 84-85, 87-88). Associated with music and Temple service; their psalms often feature Zion theology and longing for YHWH's presence.

key_terms.term: Divine Council in Hebrew primary sources
key_terms.definition: The Hebrew primary sources (Psalm 82, Iyov 1-2, Devarim 32:8 DSS text, 1 Kings 22) document YHWH presiding over an assembly of divine beings. This is the original covenant community's cosmology — not a Greek philosophical monotheism but a hierarchical structure with YHWH alone sovereign.

faq.question: What is the spiritual journey in Psalm 73 and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Psalm 73 is the most honest wrestling-with-theodicy psalm in Tehillim. Asaph nearly loses his covenant faith when the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. His resolution comes not from a logical argument but from an encounter in the sanctuary — where he sees the ultimate destiny of the wicked and recognizes that nearness to YHWH is itself the irreplaceable good. The psalm models honesty before YHWH as the first step toward restored trust.

faq.question: What does Psalm 78 accomplish as a historical recital?
faq.answer: Psalm 78 is a didactic psalm — an extended teaching meant to pass covenant memory to the next generation. It recounts Mitzrayim, the wilderness rebellions, and YHWH's repeated patience, culminating in YHWH choosing Yehudah and the sheepherder David. Its purpose is to prevent the next generation from repeating the cycle of forgetting and rebellion. It treats history as the primary teacher of covenant faithfulness.

faq.question: What is the divine council in Psalm 82 and what does it mean theologically?
faq.answer: Psalm 82 describes YHWH standing in the assembly of divine beings (elohim) and pronouncing judgment on them for failing to execute justice. These are not independent rival gods — they are beings who have been given governance roles under YHWH and have failed. YHWH's judgment strips their authority and declares their mortality. This ancient Hebrew cosmology — YHWH sovereign over a council of lesser divine beings — predates Greek monotheism's abstract formulation.

faq.question: How was Psalm 82:6 borrowed by NT writers and what is its original meaning?
faq.answer: NT writers (John 10:34-35) quoted Psalm 82:6 — 'you are elohim, sons of the Most High' — to deflect a charge of blasphemy, arguing that if the scripture calls humans 'elohim,' saying 'I am the son of YHWH' cannot be blasphemy. The original psalm uses 'elohim' for divine council members whose privilege is about to be stripped. The NT applies it to humans. Neither reading is the original context — Psalm 82:6 is a condemnation, not a promotion.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 89 end with a lament rather than praise?
faq.answer: Psalm 89 opens with YHWH's sworn covenant to maintain David's line forever and closes with a stark lament: the king is defeated, the crown lies in the dust, enemies mock. The gap between promise and reality is the crisis at Book III's close. It is an honest liturgical engagement with the experience of exile — the covenant promises have not been rescinded, but their fulfillment appears suspended. Book IV (starting Ps.90) answers this crisis with YHWH's eternal kingship.

faq.question: Who were the Sons of Korakh and what characterizes their psalms?
faq.answer: The Sons of Korakh were a Levitical musical guild descended from Korakh (Bamidbar 16). Their 11 psalms cluster in two groups (Ps.42-49 and Ps.84-88). They are strongly Zion-focused — expressing deep longing for YHWH's presence in the Temple (Ps.42-43, 84), celebrating YHWH's city (Ps.46-48), and wrestling with exile and restoration. Their psalms are characterized by intense longing and confident trust in YHWH's dwelling place.

faq.question: What makes Asaph's psalms distinctive?
faq.answer: Asaph's 12 psalms (Ps.50, 73-83) are marked by historical reflection, wrestling with injustice and divine silence, and divine council imagery (especially Ps.82). Asaph was not simply a performer but a seer — 2 Chronicles 29:30 calls him a 'seer.' His psalms tend toward the prophetic and didactic, engaging YHWH's governance of history and the problem of unresolved injustice more directly than the Davidic psalms.

faq.question: What does Psalm 84 express about longing for YHWH's presence?
faq.answer: Psalm 84 is one of the most concentrated expressions of desire for YHWH's dwelling place: the sparrow finding a home at YHWH's altars, the pilgrim whose heart sets out on the highways to Tzion, the declaration that one day in YHWH's courts surpasses a thousand elsewhere. It is the voice of exile or distance longing for the presence that makes all other goods secondary.

faq.question: How does Psalm 78's teaching about history function in the covenant community?
faq.answer: Psalm 78 functions as covenant catechesis — the extended retelling of history to prevent the cycle of forgetting, rebellion, discipline, and restoration from repeating. The opening commands parents to tell the next generation YHWH's praiseworthy acts and covenant laws. Memory is the primary defense against apostasy. The psalm demonstrates that forgetting the acts of YHWH is the root cause of every rebellion the history records.

faq.question: What is the relationship between Book III's end (Ps.89) and Book IV's beginning (Ps.90)?
faq.answer: Psalm 89 ends in lament — the Davidic covenant appears to have failed, the crown is in the dust. Psalm 90 (attributed to Moshe) responds by lifting the view from the failed dynasty to YHWH's eternal existence — 'from everlasting to everlasting, you are YHWH.' Book IV's answer to Book III's crisis is: human institutions fail; YHWH's sovereignty transcends them all. YHWH was king before David and remains king after.
